procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Supreme Court directed that writ petitions registered in High Courts regarding this matter be heard by a Division Bench constituted by the Chief Justice of the respective High Court. issue.issue_text: Expeditious disposal of criminal cases against elected members of the Parliament and Legislative Assemblies.

facts: A Public Interest Litigation was filed under Article 32 of the Constitution of India.
The petition sought the expeditious disposal of criminal cases pending against elected Members of Parliament (MPs) and Legislative Assemblies (MLAs).
The Court noted that this was not the first time it had examined this issue, referencing a previous case, Public Interest Foundation v. Union of India.
law: The case was brought under Article 32 of the Constitution of India, which allows individuals to seek remedies from the Supreme Court for the violation of fundamental rights.
application: The Supreme Court acknowledged that there was a "compelling need" to dispose of these cases expeditiously.
The Court decided to issue specific guidelines to ensure the speedy trial of these cases.
It directed the Chief Justices of all High Courts to register a suo-motu case to monitor the early disposal of criminal cases against MPs and MLAs.
The High Courts were instructed to assign these cases to an adequate number of Sessions and Magisterial Courts.
The Court established a priority system for hearing the cases: cases against sitting legislators were to be prioritized over those against former legislators.

A further priority was set based on the severity of the alleged offense: cases punishable with death or life imprisonment first, followed by those with imprisonment of 5 years or more, and then other cases.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the petitioner's prayer and issued a series of directions to the High Courts to set up a monitoring mechanism and designate courts to ensure the prioritized and speedy disposal of criminal cases against MPs and MLAs.

cases.case_name: Asian Resurfacing of Road Agency Pvt. Ltd vs. CBI
cases.principle: Trial courts are to proceed with trials notwithstanding any stay granted by the High Court, unless a fresh order is passed extending the stay by recording reasons.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Trial courts must proceed with a trial notwithstanding any stay granted by a High Court, unless a fresh, reasoned order is passed explicitly extending that stay.
obiter: To give effect to the legislative policy and the mandate of Article 21 for speedy justice in criminal cases, if a stay is granted, the matter should be taken on a day-to-day basis and concluded within two to three months.
An order of stay will stand vacated on the expiry of six months, unless an extension is granted by a speaking order showing an extraordinary situation.
The party in whose favour a stay is granted is accountable if the court ultimately finds no merit in the matter and the opposing party suffers loss and injustice.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that there is a compelling and undisputed need to expeditiously dispose of criminal cases against elected members of Parliament and Legislative Assemblies. To address delays caused by stays from higher courts, the court applied the existing legal precedent from *Asian Resurfacing of Road Agency Pvt. Ltd vs. CBI*, which mandates that a stay on trial proceedings automatically vacates after six months unless a High Court issues a fresh, reasoned order extending it. Therefore, trial courts are directed to proceed with trials unless such a specific, reasoned extension order is passed.
legal_tests_applied: The court applied the test established in *Asian Resurfacing of Road Agency Pvt. Ltd vs. CBI, 2018 (16) SCC 299*, which holds that an order of stay in a criminal trial will stand vacated on the expiry of six months, unless an extension is granted by a 'speaking order' (a reasoned order) showing an extraordinary situation where continuing the stay is preferred to the final disposal of the trial.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's prayer was accepted by the court; they did not lose. The Writ Petition was disposed of with directions aimed at achieving the relief sought.
why_respondent_won: The respondents did not 'win' as the court accepted the petitioner's core argument. The text does not detail any specific arguments from the respondents that were accepted; the court's decision was based on the acknowledged need for speedy trials and existing legal precedent.
policy_considerations: The court's decision is driven by the public policy need to give effect to the 'legislative policy and the mandate of Article 21 for speedy justice in criminal cases.'
There is a 'compelling need to take up and dispose of the subject cases expeditiously,' a point on which the court stated 'there are no two views.'
The court noted that even the accused political representatives would likely seek a quick disposal of their cases.
